Estimate the spatial autocorrelation range from data

Source: R/cross-validation.R
estimate_sac_range.Rd

Fits an exponential variogram model with a nugget and returns the effective range: three times the fitted range parameter, which is where the semivariance reaches about 95 percent of the sill. It is the distance beyond which two observations are (near) uncorrelated, which is what a block or a buffer has to exceed.

Usage

estimate_sac_range(
  points_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  n_max = 5000L,
  cutoff = 0.5,
  range_frac = 1,
  seed = 123L,
  detrend = c("ols", "reml"),
  reml_max_n = 400L,
  keep_directional_fits = FALSE,
  lags = c("adaptive", "equal"),
  n_lags = 15L,
  structure_alpha = 0.05
)

Arguments

points_sf

An sf object with point geometries (will be projected automatically if in geographic CRS). Non-POINT geometry is reduced to representative points; any Z or M dimension is dropped, because gstat::variogram() uses every coordinate dimension and an XYZ layer would otherwise return a range in 3-D while every consumer of it works in 2-D map distance; and rows with empty or non-finite coordinates are dropped with a logged count.

response_var

Character(1) name of the response column. Rows where it is missing or infinite are left out before anything else is done, so they neither take part in the choice of projection for lon/lat input nor use up the n_max subsample. For a count or other response whose variance tracks its mean, see the section on non-Gaussian responses: the range is still estimated, but it is a less reliable number than for a Gaussian response.

predictor_vars

Optional character vector. When supplied, the trend on these predictors is removed first and the variogram describes the residual autocorrelation, the part a spatial model has to handle once the covariates have done their work. How the trend is removed is set by detrend, and it matters: see "Detrending and the residual-variogram bias". Rows whose response or predictor is missing or infinite are left out of that fit, and so of the variogram, with a logged count. When that leaves fewer than 30 rows the result is the unclassed NA that says how many were left (see Value). One case differs, as it always has: when no row at all has every predictor (one is missing on every row) no trend can be fitted, and the variogram is of the raw response, with an R warning and detrended set to FALSE.

n_max

Maximum number of points the variogram is computed on, at least 30; Inf for no limit. Variogram estimation is O(n²) so this keeps runtime bounded. A layer with more rows that carry a value is cut to a seeded random subsample of this size, drawn after rows with nothing to model have been left out and with the rows in a fixed order, so the subsample does not depend on how the layer is sorted. The counts are returned as the attributes n_used, n_missing and n_subsampled.

cutoff

Fraction of the maximum inter-point distance to use as the variogram lag cutoff, above 0 and at most 1. That distance is the farthest pair, found on the convex hull, and not the bounding-box diagonal, which depends on how the axes are oriented. Default 0.5.

range_frac

Positive numeric. A fitted range exceeding range_frac * cutoff * max_dist (that is, beyond the longest lag the empirical variogram was actually fitted over) is treated as unidentified and NA_real_ is returned. A model fit yields a finite number even when the variogram never reaches a sill, and such a value extrapolates past the observed lags instead of measuring a long autocorrelation range. Passing it to make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) would collapse the block grid to a single block. Default 1.0; raise it to accept ranges extrapolated beyond the fitted lags. The bound does not guarantee room for two blocks: at the defaults it is half the farthest-pair distance, about 0.71 of the side of a square layer, and a block grid needs a range below half the width of the bounding box in one direction or the other. An accepted range between the two leaves make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) room for a single block of that size (see its auto_range argument for what it does then). Lowering range_frac to fit the grid would turn those estimates into NA and the blocks into geometric ones smaller than the range.

seed

RNG seed for the n_max subsample, restored afterwards so the caller's random stream is untouched. Default 123L: the subsample is an internal approximation and no part of the answer, and leaving it unseeded would make the returned range differ between runs on identical input and silently advance the caller's RNG. Pass NULL for an unseeded subsample, or a different number to check how sensitive the estimate is to the subsample. Ignored when no more than n_max rows carry a value, where nothing is sampled. The reml_max_n subsample uses the same seed, and so does the draw of one row a location that detrend = "reml" makes on a layer with repeat visits.

detrend

How the trend on predictor_vars is removed; ignored when there are none. "ols" (default) fits it by ordinary least squares and fits the variogram to the residuals, which underestimates the range (see the section below). "reml" fits the trend and an exponential-plus-nugget covariance together by residual maximum likelihood with nlme::gls(), returns the REML range, and attaches the empirical variogram of the REML residuals for inspection. It needs nlme, costs \(O(n^3)\), and so runs on at most reml_max_n points; when it does not converge the "ols" path runs instead with an R warning saying so. The start of the fit is chosen from the profile REML likelihood on a grid of ranges and nugget proportions, and when more than one start is fitted the fit with the largest log-likelihood is kept.

reml_max_n

Positive integer, at least 30. With detrend = "reml", the trend and covariance are fitted on a seeded random subsample of this many points when the layer has more; the fitted trend is then removed from every point. The fit takes one row a location: where a location has several rows (repeat visits), one of them is drawn at random under seed, so that the nugget fitted is the variance between visits and not that of their minimum or of their mean. Default 400. Raise it for a better-determined fit at a cubic cost.

keep_directional_fits

TRUE or FALSE. Attach each direction's empirical variogram and fitted model as directional_fits? Defaults to FALSE: the four variograms are most of the object's size, while the numbers read from them (directional, directional_fitted, directional_status, anisotropy) are attached either way, and plot() draws the effective variogram from its own attribute. Set TRUE to inspect the directional curves.

lags

How the lags are binned: "adaptive" (default) or "equal"; see "The lags" above.

n_lags

A whole number from 5 to 100, default 15. With lags = "equal", the number of bins. With lags = "adaptive", the most bins spaced geometrically past the first; fewer are used when that many would hold under 30 pairs each.

structure_alpha

The level of the test for spatial structure, above 0 and at most 1; default 0.05. A layer whose adjusted p-value is not below it gets no range. 1 switches the refusal off; the test is still computed and attached.

Value

A single number, of class sac_range in the first two of the three shapes below and an unclassed NA in the third; all three behave as an ordinary number. The shapes carry different attributes:

Success

A positive effective range in projected coordinate units, with the fit attached as attributes directional (the 0°, 45°, 90° and 135° ranges, named by azimuth; NA where that direction's fit was unusable), anisotropy (largest over smallest), anisotropy_used (always FALSE: the all-pairs fit is the estimate; kept for code that reads it), directional_status (per azimuth, why a direction is NA in directional: "ok", "over_cutoff" (its range ran past the largest lag fitted), "not_converged" (its fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched) or "no_fit" (a flat variogram, or too few bins)), directional_fitted (the range each direction's fit reported whether or not it was usable, so a refused directional range stays recoverable) and directional_fits (a list by azimuth of each direction's empirical variogram and fitted model, NULL where there is none, and NULL altogether unless keep_directional_fits = TRUE), detrended (logical: whether the variogram is of the residuals on predictor_vars or of the raw response. A missing predictor is an error, and a failed detrending fit warns and falls back to the raw response with this set to FALSE), detrend_method ("ols" or "reml" when detrended, NA otherwise), reml (with detrend = "reml": a list with n_used, subsampled, nugget_prop, sigma2, logLik (the REML log-likelihood of the fit kept), logLik_gain (its gain over the same trend with independent errors) and n_fits (the starts fitted); NULL otherwise), crs (the projected CRS the variogram was fitted in: the unit of the range), max_dist, cutoff_dist, variogram (the empirical variogram, in the units of the response's variance), variogram_model (the fitted model, in gstat's layout, or with detrend = "reml" one built from the REML parameters), nugget (that model's nugget variance; see sac_nugget), nugget_at_bound (TRUE when the nugget is at its lower bound, within 1e-4 of the sill, and so is not an estimate), first_lag (the mean separation in the first bin: the shortest lag resolved, from which the nugget is extrapolated), bins_below_range (how many bins lie inside the fitted range; with fewer than three the split between nugget and structure rests on very little), short_lag_semivariance, short_lag_pairs and short_lag_dist (the semivariance of nearest-neighbour pairs of locations with no model, their number and their median separation: an upper bound on the nugget), zero_lag_semivariance and zero_lag_pairs (the semivariance of the pairs of rows that share a location, which is the variance between visits to one place and a lower bound on the nugget, and their number; NA and 0 when no location has two rows), nugget_floor (the value the fitted nugget was not let under: zero_lag_semivariance when the rows outnumber the locations by 30 or more, else 0, and always 0 with detrend = "reml"), structure_p, morans_i and structure_test (the adjusted p-value of the test for spatial structure, Moran's I on the 8 nearest neighbours, and the statistic, z and p for each neighbourhood size), structures and short_range (how many structures the model has besides the nugget, and the effective range of the short one when there are two, NA otherwise), lags, lag_boundaries and lag_fallback (the binning behind the result, its upper bin edges, and TRUE when adaptive lags were asked for and the equal-lag result is returned; see "The lags"), and n_used, n_missing and n_subsampled (the points the variogram was computed on, the rows left out for a missing response or predictor, and the rows left out by the n_max subsample), so the fit can be inspected and need not be taken on trust.

Rejected range

NA_real_ when no range is identified. It is classed sac_range as well, so it prints as NA without dumping its attributes, and it carries every attribute of a success (the evidence for the rejection), plus rejected_range (the value that was refused, NA when none was fitted) and rejected_reason, one of:

  • "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale": the test above. The model attached is a pure nugget at the variance of the modelled variable, and nothing fitted is handed on.

  • "the empirical variogram is flat: no spatial structure at the lags resolved": no model with a range fits the variogram better than a constant. The model attached is that constant, a pure nugget.

  • "empirical variogram decreases with distance": the semivariance falls over the shorter lags (a net fall of more than 15 percent of the mean semivariance there, weighted by pairs), which is the shape of a periodic, hole-effect structure or of a variance that differs between a dense cluster and the rest of the layer. Sampling noise in the short-lag bins of a small sample can make that fall too.

  • "fitted range exceeds the largest lag fitted": the range is past range_frac * cutoff * max_dist (see range_frac). An unremoved trend ends here when the variogram rises past the fitted lags; a milder trend only lengthens the fitted range and passes, which is what predictor_vars is for.

  • "fitted range is below the shortest lag fitted": too few pairs of points lie inside the range to identify it, because it is shorter than the shortest lag the empirical variogram resolves (first_lag) or, with detrend = "reml", than the distance within which 30 pairs of the points the REML fit used lie, when that is shorter (the REML range is fitted to the point pairs, not to the bins). A structure that short cannot be told from a nugget. range_floor holds the distance the refused range fell short of.

  • "fitted range is non-positive or non-finite".

  • "no variogram model could be fitted (singular fits)": fewer than three lag bins hold point pairs. variogram_model is NULL and nugget is NA.

The reason names one ground for the refusal, in the order above. attr(attr(range, "variogram_model"), "converged") says one thing more about the model: it is FALSE when the least-squares criterion is still falling at an edge of the ranges searched (a variogram with no sill inside four cutoffs), and the nugget and sill of such a model are that edge and not fitted values. For a model with two structures the flag is that of the equal-lag fit the long range came from: when that fit has no minimum, the long structure's range and partial sill are the edge of its search and the flag is FALSE, although the nugget and the short structure were fitted at the adaptive lags. A model built from REML parameters carries no such attribute. resolution_profile() reads it, and takes no nugget from a model marked FALSE. Results stored by earlier versions can carry "variogram model did not converge" as their reason and anisotropy_used = TRUE; neither is produced any more.

No fit

An unclassed NA_real_ when estimation could not be attempted at all, whose one attribute, rejected_reason, says why: "package 'gstat', which the variogram needs, is not installed", "<n> points, fewer than the 30 a variogram range is estimated from", "<n> point(s) with a finite value to model, fewer than the 30 a variogram range is estimated from" (the count is of the whole layer's rows with a value), "the response is constant", "the residuals on predictor_vars are constant: the predictors explain the response exactly" or "the points have no extent (the largest distance between them is zero or could not be computed)". Nothing is fitted, so none of the other attributes above exist: no variogram, variogram_model or rejected_range, which is what tells it from a range that was fitted and refused.

Attributes and the class do not affect is.na() or is.finite(), so every downstream guard treats all three the same way it always did.

Details

The result is a function of the data alone. The same layer gives the same answer whatever the unit of the response or of the coordinates and whatever the order of its rows, and a change in the last bits of the values changes the answer by about as much. Three things make it so. The rows are sorted by their coordinates as supplied, then by the response and the predictors, before anything else, so the projection chosen for lon/lat input, the n_max subsample and the pair sums do not depend on their order. (Rows that share a location are therefore in the order of their values, and no step treats the first of them as special.) The variogram is computed on the standardised variable, and a response is called constant only when its standard deviation is under 1e-12 of its largest absolute value, which no change of unit alters. And the model is fitted without iteration: the criterion is gstat's weighted least squares (weights \(N / h^2\)) on lags divided by the cutoff; for each trial range the nugget and the partial sill are solved exactly, with both kept at or above zero; and the range is found by a search over a logarithmic grid from a quarter of the first lag to four cutoffs, refined in one dimension. There is no start value, no iteration limit and no fit that fails to converge.

Only the exponential family is fitted. On fields smoother than exponential that makes the range long, which is the safe side (blocks too large, cross-validation pessimistic). Choosing the family by the smaller weighted sum of squares would correct a spherical field but send exponential fields low, the direction that leaks.

Spatial structure is tested first. A variogram model can be fitted to anything, and on a layer with no structure the fit returns a finite range for a large share of draws. So Moran's I of the modelled variable is computed on its 2, 4, 8 and 16 nearest neighbours, each standardised with the moments that fit the variable (those of regression residuals when predictor_vars are given), and the smallest one-sided p-value is multiplied by four. When that adjusted p-value is not below structure_alpha, the result is NA with rejected_reason "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale", a pure-nugget model and no fitted range. The test uses no random numbers. structure_p, morans_i and structure_test are attached to every classed result. Measured on a 1000 m square with 300 points, the test refuses 388 of 400 white-noise layers and 8 get a finite range, against 196 with the test off. Its power is limited where few neighbours lie inside the range. With a nugget of a fifth of the sill it finds structure in 88 percent of fields of effective range 60 on 300 points, and in 21 percent at range 30, which is about the spacing of those points. A short range on a sparse layer can therefore be refused; structure_alpha = 1 switches the refusal off. Rows that share a location (repeat visits) are one place and not each other's neighbours, so on such a layer the test is made on the means of the locations: what it asks is whether locations near each other are alike, which a location's own effect, however large, does not answer. With very unequal numbers of visits the p-value is approximate.

The lags. With lags = "adaptive" (the default) the first bin runs from zero to the distance within which the closest max(50, n / 4) pairs of distinct locations lie, and up to n_lags further bins are spaced geometrically from there to the cutoff; a bin holding fewer than 30 pairs is merged with the next. The short lags are then resolved at the spacing of the points, which is what the nugget and a short range are read from. With lags = "equal" there are n_lags bins of equal width out to the cutoff, as gstat bins by default; each is cutoff * max_dist / n_lags wide, a structure shorter than the first of them is invisible and is counted as nugget, and the range fitted is that of whatever longer structure the layer has. Below about a hundred points neither binning resolves much and the adaptive bins bring no gain.

Two rows at one location are a pair at zero separation, and are in no bin, whichever the binning: the variogram and the model describe positive separations. Their semivariance, the variance between visits to a location, is returned on its own as zero_lag_semivariance, and the nugget fitted to the variogram is not let under it when the layer has 30 or more rows beyond one a location to estimate it from (a model from detrend = "reml" takes no such floor); see sac_nugget.

The adaptive lags put little weight on the long ones, and a weak, long structure under much noise can be clear at equal lags while the adaptive fit runs past the largest lag. So when the adaptive range is refused as past the fitted lags and the equal-lag fit has a range it would itself return, the result is the equal-lag one, whole, exactly as lags = "equal" gives it, with lags saying "equal" and lag_fallback set to TRUE. Its nugget is then the equal-lag nugget. No other refusal falls back.

Structure at two scales. One structure fitted to lags that resolve the spacing of the points follows the shortest structure of the layer. A layer can have a weaker structure several times longer as well, and blocks sized from the short one would leave the long one across folds. So with lags = "adaptive" the equal-lag fit is made too, and when its range is at least twice the adaptive one, a model with a nugget and both structures, at those two ranges, is fitted to the adaptive variogram. That model is returned (structures is 2 and short_range holds the range of the short structure) and the range is the long one, unless the long structure carries under 3 percent of the model's semivariance at the largest lag: then the lags that resolve the layer give the equal-lag range nothing, and the single structure stands. The bar is low because the two mistakes are not alike. A long structure that is missed sizes blocks too small, which leaks. One that is believed in error returns the equal-lag range, which is too long and makes a validation pessimistic, and short_range still holds the short one. When the equal-lag range is one that lags = "equal" would itself refuse (past the fitted lags, as under an unremoved trend), the model with it is refused as well, the answer is taken away and not lengthened, and the long structure has to carry 10 percent.

Measured on a clustered layer of 1200 points over a 1000 m square, 30 draws each. With structures of range 20 and 200 both are kept in 20 draws, and the range returned is under half the equal-lag one in 1; with 40 and 400, in 18 and 1; with 30 and 300, in 21 and 0; with 15 and 450, in 28 and 1. With one structure of range 40 a second is kept in 4, and the range is within a factor 2 of the truth in 27 draws (19 with equal lags); with one of range 30, in 7 and 25 (14). The nugget comes from the adaptive lags either way: where it is 0.3, the median is 0.32 to 0.35, and 0.49 to 0.65 with equal lags. A long structure whose equal-lag range is under twice the adaptive one is not separated: the range is then that of the single fit, which lies between the two.

The estimate is the omnidirectional (all-pairs) fit. Directional variograms are fitted as well, at 0° (N–S), 45°, 90° (E–W) and 135° azimuths with a ±22.5° tolerance. Those four windows tile all 180 distinct azimuths exactly once, and their ranges are returned in the directional attribute, with their largest-over-smallest ratio in anisotropy. They are a diagnostic and never the answer, for two reasons. Each direction sees about a quarter of the point pairs, and the maximum of four quarter-sample fits is biased upward. And the windows are fixed to the coordinate axes, so any answer built from them changes when the layer is rotated, which a property of the field must not do. The all-pairs fit is the best-powered estimate available and is invariant to rotation. When it identifies no range, no range is returned: the largest directional range does not stand in for it.

Where a field is known to be anisotropic, blocks must be at least as large as the longest autocorrelation range to avoid leakage, and the conservative choice is to size them from the longest directional range explicitly. Read it from directional_fitted, not directional: on a strongly anisotropic field the major axis is the direction most likely to run past the fitted lags, which leaves it NA in directional, so max() of that is NA, or with na.rm = TRUE the second-longest range. Check directional_status first: a major axis marked "over_cutoff" has no identified range at all, and a longer cutoff or make_folds(method = "nndm") is the way on. A ratio above 1.5 is written to the package log at INFO level with that advice, which reaches the session log file but not the console (the ratio passes 1.5 on most isotropic fields too); print() shows the directional ranges and the ratio, and attr(range, "anisotropy") holds it.

A direction whose variogram is flat or has too few bins, whose range runs beyond the longest fitted lag, or whose fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched is excluded and recorded as NA in the directional attribute.

The model is fitted with a nugget. A nugget-free model forces the curve through the origin, and on any real measurement (which has one) the \(N / h^2\) weights buy that constraint by collapsing the range. The fitted nugget can sit at its lower bound of zero; the result then carries nugget_at_bound = TRUE, and sac_nugget says what else is attached to judge a nugget by.

The returned range is in the coordinate units of the (projected) data and can be passed directly to make_folds(block_size = ...) so that CV blocks are at least as wide as the autocorrelation range.

Detrending and the residual-variogram bias

Fitting a variogram to the residuals of a least-squares trend underestimates both the sill and the range, because the trend fit absorbs part of the long-wavelength spatial variation (Lark, Cullis and Welham 2006). Blocks sized from that range are then too small and a blocked validation is less conservative than it claims. How large the effect is depends on how smooth the trend terms are in space, and on how many there are: for ordinary covariates it is a few percent, and for trend surfaces in the coordinates it is large. Iterating between a GLS trend fit and a variogram refit (Neuman and Jacobson 1984) recovers only part of it, because the variogram of GLS residuals is biased too; REML does not fit a variogram to residuals at all, which is why detrend = "reml" returns its own range estimate. Its price is a single family (exponential with nugget), a cubic cost in n, and a somewhat wider sampling spread. The default stays "ols" so that existing scripts keep their method; a script that detrends on smooth or coordinate-based terms should pass detrend = "reml", or size its blocks with a margin. Detrending removes a trend the predictors explain. It does not make an unidentified range identified.

Count and other non-Gaussian responses

The empirical variogram assumes second-order stationarity: a variance that is the same everywhere, so that semivariance depends on separation alone. A count response breaks that assumption by construction, because its variance tracks its mean, and so does any response with a mean-variance relationship (rates, proportions, skewed amounts). On such data the variogram mixes distance-dependence with mean-dependence, and the fitted range is not the thing it claims to be: where the mean is high the semivariance is inflated whatever the distance, which flattens the curve and can lengthen or shorten the apparent range depending on where the high-mean regions sit.

Supplying predictor_vars to detrend helps, because it removes the part of the mean the covariates explain, but it does not fix the variance structure: the residuals of an OLS fit to a count still have a variance that tracks the fitted mean. The principled remedy is a variogram of Pearson residuals from a model in the right family, which this function does not compute. Treat the range from a count response as no more than an order of magnitude, size blocks conservatively from it, and prefer make_folds(method = "nndm"), which does not depend on a fitted range at all.

References

Cliff, A. D. and Ord, J. K. (1981). Spatial Processes: Models and Applications. Pion, London.

Lark, R. M., Cullis, B. R. and Welham, S. J. (2006). On spatial prediction of soil properties in the presence of a spatial trend: the empirical best linear unbiased predictor (E-BLUP) with REML. European Journal of Soil Science, 57(6), 787–799. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2389.2005.00768.x

Neuman, S. P. and Jacobson, E. A. (1984). Analysis of nonintrinsic spatial variability by residual kriging with application to regional groundwater levels. Mathematical Geology, 16(5), 499–521. doi:10.1007/BF01886329

See also

sac_nugget for the nugget behind the estimate, plot.sac_range to see the variogram the estimate rests on.

Other cross-validation: area_of_applicability(), cv_bayes(), cv_block_size_sweep(), cv_gwr(), cv_rf(), cv_spatial(), fold_separation(), gwr_model_selection(), make_folds(), sac_nugget(), select_features_forward()

Examples

if (requireNamespace("gstat", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(sf)
  # A Gaussian random field with an exponential covariance: range
  # parameter 100, so the true effective range is 3 x 100 = 300, plus a
  # small nugget.
  set.seed(9)
  n <- 150
  xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
  D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
  xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 100) + diag(0.1, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
  pts <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
  r <- estimate_sac_range(pts, response_var = "z")
  # print() throughout, because only the last value of a braced block is
  # shown on its own, and every one of these is worth reading.
  print(r)                              # the effective range, in metres
  print(attr(r, "directional"))         # the four directional ranges
  print(attr(r, "variogram_model"))     # the fitted model behind it
  print(attr(r, "structure_p"))         # the test for spatial structure

  # A field whose range the data cannot pin down: the variogram never
  # reaches a sill within the lags fitted, so the answer is NA with the
  # refused value attached rather than a long range asserted.
  xy$trend <- sin(xy$x / 400) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2)
  r2 <- estimate_sac_range(st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632),
                           response_var = "trend")
  print(r2)
  attr(r2, "rejected_reason")
  attr(r2, "rejected_range")

  # White noise: no structure, so no range.
  xy$noise <- rnorm(n)
  r3 <- estimate_sac_range(st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632),
                           response_var = "noise")
  attr(r3, "rejected_reason")
}
#> 292.1814 
#>   directional: 0 deg = 248.1608, 45 deg = 413.7318, 90 deg = 617.9676, 135 deg = 426.5880  (ratio 2.49)
#>   in metres of EPSG:32632; variogram of the response itself
#>        0       45       90      135 
#> 248.1608 413.7318 617.9676 426.5880 
#>   model    psill    range
#> 1   Nug 0.000000  0.00000
#> 2   Exp 1.273642 97.39379
#> [1] 8.510444e-22
#> NA 
#>   directional: 0 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags), 45 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags), 90 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags), 135 deg = 2672.119 (past the fitted lags)
#>   in metres of EPSG:32632; variogram of the response itself
#> [1] "no spatial structure detected at the nearest-neighbour scale"
